input.text: Zhihua Temple is a Ming dynasty time capsule with a soundtrack. It was built in fourteen forty-four by Wang Zhen, the most powerful court eunuch of his age — ostensibly a family temple, built, some said, in defiance of rules that eunuchs should build none. Its roofs wear black glazed tiles — a color rank reserved for special favor — and its halls survive almost untouched, one of the most complete Ming wooden temple complexes in the city. Its greater treasure is heard, not seen: Zhihua Temple's Music, the Beijing "jing music" performed by monk lineages for over five hundred years, passed mouth-to-ear across generations and now listed as national intangible heritage. Short recitals are still played here on selected days — sit in a fifteenth-century hall and hear Ming-dynasty sound. Hutong-quiet, crowd-free, and unforgettable: this is old Beijing's most scholarly secret.
